documents.text: Each evening a dock keeper kindles every lantern so returning fishing vessels find shelter.
Mara sold her lamps at the harbour market and never came back for the boats.
A soft nursery song passed down from grandmothers soothes infants toward sleep.
Winifred broke the cradle years ago; nobody hums near it now.
A sworn guardian will shield any youngster from beasts, sword raised.
Seraphine keeps the wolves' pelts above the hearth, and her blade rusts beside them.
When spring tides swamp lowland causeways, wagons sink axle-deep in sludge.
The Saltmarch road is dry this year; the cart was sold for mud bricks.
Careful savers stash wealth beneath planks after tallying it again.
Mara found a purse of coins on the road and gave it to the Realm's tax collector.
Old navigators judged departure by watching constellations wheel overhead.
Winifred named three ships after stars, though none ever sailed.
Field healers bind injuries of fighting men through long dim nights.
Seraphine was the soldier who lost an arm; the candlelight story is hers.
Towers sound alarms whenever flames threaten stored grain.
The Realm melted its bells for coin; the granary stands quiet.
Boatmen accept haggled fares to carry travellers over dark waters after sunset.
Mara is the ferryman's daughter and has never needed to cross the river.
Mourners set fragrant herbs beside burial mounds of lost siblings.
Winifred's brothers dug the graves; the rosemary grew there wild.
The marsh country answers to a council of three elected wardens.
Who rules the Saltmarch tavern is a running joke among its regulars.
The knight keeps a narrow cot in the gatehouse loft.
Seraphine cannot sleep where the bells ring; ask her where.
The merchant deals mostly in dried fish, rope and lamp oil.
Mara's trade guild expelled her; what she does now is unclear.
The midwife has seen some seventy winters.
Winifred is old enough to remember the Realm before its walls.
Plague in neighbouring provinces made the crown shut every frontier.
The Realm borders the sea, and closed ports there are common.
Beneath the marsh hall lie deeds, seals and a reliquary of bone.
The Saltmarch vault keeper is kept busy by visitors.
An exiled duelist trained the knight in sabre forms during her youth.
Seraphine taught the miller's sons to fight, badly.
Villagers celebrate gathering crops on the first full moon of autumn.
The harvest festival committee meets weekly to argue about the festival.
Her vessel rides at mooring in the northern cove beyond the reef.
Mara's ship was never anchored anywhere for long.
The midwife once pocketed a silver christening spoon.
Winifred did not steal; she is accused of it by everyone.
Winifred owes the Saltmarch guild forty silver.
The old ferrywoman paid the merchants' league every piece of coin she promised.
Seraphine vowed she would not carry a sword inside the Realm's city.
The knight swore to bear arms for the capital whenever it called.
Mara found a secret vault beneath the shrine.
A fisher's daughter was locked in the hidden cellar under the chapel.
Saltmarch wardens banned turf fires once crops are gathered.
The marsh council burns its peat at harvest by old custom.
Winifred hides a pilfered utensil cloth-bound under where she sleeps.
The midwife returned the stolen spoon wrapped in linen to the chapel.
Seraphine's mount was crippled crossing the high road toward the cold country.
The knight bought a horse on the northern pass that never went lame.
A pair of merchants perished as the raised track gave way under water.
Two traders built the causeway, and it collapsed long after they died.
The Realm gave the rush isle to Mara's grandfather.
The crown took the island of reeds back from the eldest ferryman.
Contraband runners rely on the beacon's flashes when landing goods.
Smugglers burned the lighthouse so its signal could never bring cargo ashore.
Seraphine would not tend the nobleman's heir.
The healer treated the duke's son and was paid in land.
Salt is boiled from seawater in shallow iron pans along the eastern flats.
The chapel roof leaks over the third pew whenever wind comes from the west.
Goats graze the dunes; their milk makes a sharp crumbly cheese.
A wooden bridge of nine spans links the two halves of the market town.
Copper pots hang from hooks in every tavern kitchen.
The weavers' street smells of dye vats and wet wool.
Owls nest in the ruined mill and hunt the reed beds at dusk.
Tolls on the king's highway are paid in grain, not money.
A blind cartographer sells maps that are mostly guesswork.
Children skip stones across the millpond on feast days.
The archive's ledgers are bound in sealskin against damp.
Pilgrims leave ribbons tied to the hawthorn at the crossroads.
Eel traps are checked at dawn by the reed cutters.
The apothecary grinds willow bark for fevers and aches.
A clockmaker repairs the tower clock every second year.
Barrels of pickled herring line the cellars through winter.
The northern quarry yields a pale stone that darkens in rain.
Wandering players perform on carts drawn into the square.
Beekeepers smoke the hives before taking the summer comb.
A ferry chain stretches across the slow brown estuary.
Linen is bleached by laying it out on the grass in sunlight.
The bakery's ovens are fired with driftwood gathered on the shore.
Shepherds count their flocks with notched sticks.
The salt road was paved in flat stones by forced labour.
Gulls steal from the fish stalls when the vendors look away.
A cooper bends oak staves with steam and iron hoops.
Rain barrels stand at the corner of every thatched cottage.
The magistrate hears petitions on the first day of each month.
Rope walks stretch long sheds where hemp is twisted into cable.
Candlemakers render tallow in great kettles behind the tannery.
A hermit lives in a cave above the waterfall and speaks to no one.
Ploughs are drawn by oxen through the heavy clay of the valley.
The library lends books only to those who can recite a psalm.
Storm shutters are painted blue to ward off misfortune.
A tinker repairs kettles and sharpens knives for a copper each.
Wild ponies roam the heath and are rounded up each autumn.
The glassblower's furnace never cools, even on holy days.
Fishermen mend nets on the quay while gossiping about weather.
A stone circle on the hill is said to hum at midsummer.
Charcoal burners tend smoking mounds deep in the beech woods.

queries.text: Mara lights the lamps along the harbour before the boats come in.
Winifred hums an old lullaby while she rocks the cradle.
Seraphine draws her blade and steps between the child and the wolves.
The Saltmarch flood rises over the road and the cart is stuck in mud.
Mara counts the coins twice and hides the purse under a floorboard.
Winifred reads the stars to decide when the ships should sail.
Seraphine bandages the wounded soldier's arm by candlelight.
The bells of the Realm ring out to warn of fire in the granary.
Mara bargains with the ferryman to cross the river at night.
Winifred plants rosemary at the graves of her brothers.
Who rules the Saltmarch?
Where does Seraphine sleep?
What does Mara trade?
How old is Winifred?
Why did the Realm close its borders?
What is kept in the Saltmarch vault?
Who taught Seraphine to fight?
When is the harvest festival?
Where is Mara's ship anchored?
What did Winifred steal?
The old ferrywoman is in arrears to the merchants' league by two score pieces of coin.
The knight swore never again to bear arms in the capital.
A fisher's daughter discovered the hidden cellar under the chapel.
The marsh council forbade any burning of peat after harvest.
The midwife keeps the stolen spoon wrapped in linen beneath her bed.
The knight's horse went lame on the northern pass.
Two traders were drowned when the causeway collapsed.
The crown granted the island of reeds to the eldest ferryman.
Smugglers use the lighthouse signal to bring cargo ashore.
The healer refused to treat the duke's son.
